div.l: WHan that Aprill with his shoures soote
The drought of Marche hath ꝑpershed þe roote
And bathed eủery veyn in swiche licour
Of soche v̉ertue engendred is þe floure
And zepherus eke with his swete breth
Enspired hath in eủery holt and heth
The tendre croppes and the yonge son̄
Hath in the Ram half his cours ron̄
And smale foules make melody
That slepe all night wᵗith open Ie
So prekketh hem nature in her corage
Than longeth yt folk to go on pilgremage
And Palmers for to seche straunge strondes
To ferne halowes couthe in sondry londes
And specially from eủery shires ende
Of Engelond to Caunterbury þei wende
The holy blisful martir for to seke
That hem hath holp when they were seke
So byfyll yt þat seson on̄ a day
In southwerk at þe Tabard as I lay
Redy to wende on̄ my pilgremage
To Caunterbury wᵗith full deuoute corage
That night was come in to oure ostry
Wele xxix in a cumpany
Of diủers folk by auenture yfall
In felyship̄ and pilgrymes were they all
And toward Caunterbury wold þei ryde
The chambres and stables weren wyde
And wele were we esed at the best
And shortly when þe son̄ went to rest
So hade I spoke with hem eilychone
That I was of her felyshipp̄ anone
And made foreward erly to ryse
To take our wey as I shall yoᵘ deuise
But neủertheles while I haue tyme and space
Er þat I in þis tale ferther pace
Me thinketh yt accordyng were to resoıı̄un
To telle yoᵘ all the condicoıı̄un
Of ecch of hem so as it semeth me
And whiche they were and of what degre
